ASML NA
THE RESEARCH TEAM ON MANAGEMENT

Management and capital allocation: President and CEO Christophe Fouquet joined ASML in 2008 and held several management positions in marketing and product management prior to CEO, including Chief Business Officer from 2022 to 2024, EVP of EUV from 2018 to 2022 and EVP of Applications from 2013 to 2018. Prior to ASML, he worked at industry peers KLA Tencor and Applied Materials. Executives are long-tenured with decades of accumulated technical knowledge. While CFO Roger Dassen comes from a pure finance and audit background (previously at Deloitte), there are mostly engineers at the top (the CEO has a physics background, and the CTO is a mathematician). On capital allocation, the hierarchy follows a fairly classic framework for a capital-light, high-margin industrial business. Priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business, with R&D treated as sacrosanct and cap ex spend to scale production capacity, and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. Over the last three decades, they’ve spent nearly €34bn on a cumulative basis on R&D, which is consistently low- to mid-teens as a percent of total sales. This spend is not discretionary, but rather the engine that sustains the monopoly. Since the mid-1990s, ASML has spent nearly €15bn on cap ex on a cumulative basis (typically mid- to high-single-digits as a percent of sales) to ensure sufficient manufacturing capacity to build enough machines to meet demand. ASML has returned €16.7bn in dividends over the last two decades, and they’ve repurchased €28.2bn in stock over that same time frame. Nearly 75% of buybacks have occurred in the last five years. While M&A is not a priority, ASML has made selective, strategic acquisitions over time, mostly to internalize critical technology dependencies (for example, acquiring Cymer for their industry leading laser light sources).

Source: ASML research pack 5_5_2026
